---
title: "Architecture"
guide-section: "Understanding replaylab"
---

# Architecture overview

replaylab decides **which designed proteins to test in a wet lab**. A pool of
designs has predicted metrics; an agent buys batches under a budget, results
come back (immediately or after a delay), and the agent decides what to buy
next and when to stop. Every strategy is validated offline by **replaying**
recorded real outcomes (Adaptyv's Proteinbase data); the same code is meant to
drive a live campaign later.

# Data flow
 
The following charts summarize the data flow in replaylab.

*Build phase*
```{d2}
direction: right

csv: "proteinbase.csv"

tables: {
  label: "build_tables"
  designs: "designs (parquet)"
  outcomes: "outcomes (parquet)"
  targets: "targets (parquet)"
}

derived: {
  label: "derived tables"
  clusters: "clusters.csv"
  folds: "folds.csv"
}

pool: "DesignPool\n(visible features)"
hidden: "hidden outcomes"

csv -> tables
tables -> derived
tables -> pool
tables -> hidden
```

## Derived tables: clusters and folds

Both files in that box come from `data/build_clusters.py` and
`data/build_folds.py`, are committed under `data/splits/`, and are then treated
as frozen: `--check` only prints `OK` or `DIFF` against the committed summary,
and rewriting one deliberately takes `--force`.

**Clusters: which designs are the same design, twice.** Each sequence becomes a
binary 3-mer vector (`kmer_matrix`), and designs within cosine distance 0.4 of
each other are joined into one *cluster* -- the connected components of that
pair graph. Sequences that close are almost always the same family, often the
same author, so a cluster is this repo's unit of "variants of one thing".
Clusters do two jobs, both offline:

* **cutting the split** (next paragraph): a family is never divided across
  folds, so no design's cousins sit in the development games while it sits in
  the held-out set;
* **scoring**: `ScoreCard.distinct_families` counts how many clusters the hits
  came from -- four hits from one family is a different result from four
  families.

Clusters never reach a decision: they live on `DesignPool` and in the scoring
context, not on `CampaignState`, and no tool can return one. What an agent gets
instead is `similar_designs` -- the same 3-mer geometry, computed live from the
campaign's designs and returned as similarity values only.

**Folds: the train/test cut.** Every design of a target lands in one of three
folds, assigned with `StratifiedGroupKFold` where the *group* is its cluster
(family integrity) and the *label* is its hit (equal hit rates). The builder
tries seeds until one split puts all three folds within ±2 designs and ±2 hits
of each other. **Fold 2 is the held-out fold**, which gives the three splits in
`config/games.yaml`: `dev` = folds 0 and 1, `heldout` = fold 2, and `all` ignores
folds entirely (the stop games, `E`, `E-long`).

So `folds.csv` *is* the train/test split, frozen and committed instead of drawn
at run time. That is why it is an argument to `build_replay_campaign`: it
decides **which designs the game contains** -- `load_pool` and `load_outcomes`
both filter through it -- and no model is cross-validated on it; a model is fit
only on what a campaign has actually bought.

*Campaign phase*
```{d2}
direction: right

inputs: {
  pool: "DesignPool"
  clusters: "clusters"
  folds: "folds"
  hidden: "hidden outcomes"
}

vars: {
  d2-config: {
    layout-engine: elk
  }
}

env: "build_replay_campaign\n(aliases by seed)"
state: "CampaignState\nsnapshot"
batch: "batch of\ndesign ids"
submit: "Campaign.submit\n(ticks the clock,\nstores events)"
backend: "Backend.poll\n(outcomes arrive)"
score: "settle + score"
card: "ScoreCard"

inputs.pool -> env
inputs.clusters -> env
inputs.folds -> env
inputs.hidden -> env
env -> state
state -> batch: policy chooses\na batch
batch -> submit
submit -> backend
backend -> state
submit -> score
score -> card
```

# Layers
```{d2}
direction: right

classes: {
  module: {
    width: 170
    style.font-size: 13
  }
}

vars: {
  d2-config: {
    layout-engine: elk
  }
}

world: "The world" {
  direction: down

  engine: "engine (game rules)"
  store: "store (SQLite)"
  backends: "backends\n(deliver outcomes)"
  datasets: "datasets"
  config: "config (YAML loading)"
  domain: "domain (core types)\nstdlib only -- imports nothing"

  engine -> store
  engine -> backends
  engine -> datasets
  engine -> config
  store -> domain
  backends -> domain
  datasets -> domain
  datasets -> config
  config -> domain
}

agent: "The agent" {
  direction: down

  policies: "policies"
  advisor: "advisor"

  policies -> advisor
}

eval: "eval"

# the agent-facing layer: imports every lane, and nothing imports it
interfaces: "interfaces\n(14 tools: MCP server + CLI)"

world.engine.class: module
world.store.class: module
world.backends.class: module
world.datasets.class: module
world.config.class: module
world.domain.class: module

agent.policies.class: module
agent.advisor.class: module

eval.class: module
interfaces.class: module

agent.policies -> world.domain
agent.advisor -> world.domain
agent.advisor -> world.datasets
eval -> world.engine { style.stroke-dash: 4 }
eval -> agent.policies { style.stroke-dash: 4 }
interfaces -> world
interfaces -> agent
```

In this chart the arrows are **imports, not data flow**: `a -> b` means package
`a` may import package `b`, which is exactly the map
`tests/test_import_boundaries.py` enforces (dashed edges: `eval` drives that
layer and may import anything). The lane that reaches both sides is
`interfaces` -- the 14 tools, the MCP server and the command line: it may
import every package shown here, and none of them may import it back (the same
boundary test, which exempts `eval`, the driver). Every arrow ends at `domain`
because `domain` imports nothing from replaylab -- standard library only. It holds the shared
vocabulary (`Design`, `Outcome`, `CampaignState`, the feature specs) that all
the other packages are written in, so it is the floor everything stands on,
not a funnel things flow into.

The split is not cosmetic: `tests/test_import_boundaries.py` fails the build
if a package imports outside its lane.

::: {.callout-note}
**The rule that matters:** `advisor` and `policies` never import `store`,
`backends` or `engine`. They receive a
[`CampaignState`](../reference/domain.CampaignState.qmd) snapshot and nothing
else, so they *cannot* write and *cannot* see outcomes the campaign has not
bought. That is the architectural half of the leak protection; the rest is
below.
:::

# Persistence and kill-and-resume

The [`CampaignStore`](../reference/store.CampaignStore.qmd) (SQLite) records
every mutation as one transaction, and batches only ever move forward:
`proposed → submitted → partial → complete`. Alongside the tables there is an
**append-only event log**. `build_replay_campaign` replays that log to
reconstruct the replay backend's exact state, so a process that is killed mid
campaign picks up where it stopped and ends in *exactly* the same state as an
uninterrupted run (verified for delay 0 and delay 2).

# The leak rules

Hidden outcomes must never reach a strategy before it buys the design. Three
independent layers enforce this:

1. **Architecture** — the import boundaries above; policies only see snapshots.
2. **API shape** — the [`ReplayBackend`](../reference/backends.ReplayBackend.qmd)
   serves an outcome only via `Campaign.submit` + `ReplayBackend.poll` after its delay; there is no
   bulk accessor to leak through.
3. **Guards** — `load_outcomes` refuses to read the held-out split outside the
   final run (`HeldOutAccessError`), and the evaluation runner refuses
   held-out games with `ValueError`. Real ids never appear in state or in any
   file the store writes: agents see `d0001`-style aliases.

# Determinism

No global random state, no `hash()` of strings, no dependence on dict or set
ordering for output. Randomness comes only from a seeded
`numpy.random.Generator` that is passed in (`make_rng(seed, round)`), so the
same state and the same seed always produce the same batch — which is what
makes 100-seed evaluation tables reproducible.
